33 A voltmeter connected between two points P and Q in an electrical circuit shows a reading of 1 V.
V
+
–
P
Q
Which statement is correct?
A
The energy needed to move +1 C of charge from P to Q is 1 J.
B
The energy needed to move +1 C of charge from Q to P is 1 J.
C
The energy needed to move one electron from P to Q is 1 J.
D
The energy needed to move one electron from Q to P is 1 J.

hints: Notice the voltmeter signs in the diagram: the + terminal is at P and the - terminal is at Q, so P is $1 \text{ V}$ higher in potential than Q.
Recall $V = W/Q$, so $1 \text{ V}$ means $1 \text{ J}$ per $1 \text{ C}$ moved between the points, not per electron.
Think about which direction needs work done on a positive charge: moving with the drop in potential or moving against it from the - side to the + side?
walkthrough: Look at the diagram: the voltmeter reads $1 \text{ V}$ with + at P and - at Q, so $V_P - V_Q = 1 \text{ V}$ and P is at the higher potential.
State the definition of potential difference: $V = W/Q$, where $W$ is the work done moving charge $Q$ between the points.
For $Q = +1 \text{ C}$ and $V = 1 \text{ V}$, the energy transferred is $W = VQ = 1 \times 1 = 1 \text{ J}$.
Decide the direction: work must be done on a positive charge to move it from low potential to high potential, so from Q to P, while P to Q would release energy.
Options with one electron are wrong because the electron charge is $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, giving energy $e \times 1 \text{ V}$ which is far smaller than $1 \text{ J}$. This is option B

A.explanation: P is at higher potential than Q, so a positive charge moving from P to Q loses energy rather than needing $1 \text{ J}$ of work done on it.

B.explanation: Moving $+1 \text{ C}$ up the potential from Q to P needs $W = VQ = 1 \times 1 = 1 \text{ J}$ of work.

C.explanation: One electron has charge of only $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so moving it through $1 \text{ V}$ transfers about $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$, not $1 \text{ J}$.

D.explanation: The charge magnitude is wrong for $1 \text{ J}$, and a negative electron moving from Q to P would lose energy because P is positive relative to Q.
